claims.subject: Amateur observers
claims.text: Some amateur observers contribute to science by participating in citizen science projects such as monitoring variable stars, double stars, sunspots, and occultations, as well as discovering transient events like comets, galactic novae, or supernovae. This contribution occurs even though amateur astronomy is not their primary source of income or professional field.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: Although scientific research may not be their primary goal, some amateur astronomers contribute to citizen science by monitoring variable stars,[1] double stars,[2] sunspots,[3] and occultations of stars by the Moon[4] or asteroids,[4] as well as by discovering transient astronomical events, such as comets,[5] galactic novae[6] or supernovae in other galaxies.[7]

references.label: P2.1
references.text: Amateur astronomers do not use the field of astronomy as their primary source of income or support, as well as typically having no professional degree in astrophysics or advanced academic training in the subject.

Question: How can some amateur observers contribute to science while astronomy is not their primary income?
Subject: Amateur observers
Some amateur observers contribute to science by participating in citizen science projects such as monitoring variable stars, double stars, sunspots, and occultations, as well as discovering transient events like comets, galactic novae, or supernovae. This contribution occurs even though amateur astronomy is not their primary source of income or professional field. [1]
